title: Why do we believe in urban legends?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss urban legends and why people believe and pass them along. They open with a bogus National Gang Week baby-in-the-road warning and the headlight-flashing gang myth, then cover the Vegas kidney-theft story (and its link to the real Mohammed Salim Khan kidney case), the hook-killer parking legend, legends as cautionary tales reflecting shifting morality, fear and regionalization, "friend of a friend" hallmarks, the Eddie Murphy/Reggie Jackson elevator legend, news-sourced and movie/TV-sourced legends, folklore history (Fitzgerald, Brunvand's Encyclopedia of Urban Legends), Snopes debunking, Halloween poisoned candy, forwarded-email hoaxes (Neiman Marcus cookies, birther email), and true-but-strange stories (the Elmer McCurdy mummy in a carnival fun house). The episode ends with a plug list of sister podcasts and blogs instead of listener mail.

segments.title: Opening banter and gang-week hoax
segments.summary: Casual banter about lunch and a Gang Week story that Josh says is a made-up warning about a fake baby left on the roadside to lure female motorists. Police departments reportedly could not verify it. Also mentioned is a headlight-flashing gang myth.

segments.title: Vegas kidney legend and cautionary tales
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Las Vegas kidney-theft legend and note that a real kidney-removal case (Mohammed Salim Khan) made it feel plausible. They explain that urban legends are often cautionary tales with a moral twist, and the hook-killer parking legend from the 1950s is used to show how the morals shift over time.

segments.title: Why legends reflect fears and spread
segments.summary: Urban legends mostly reflect fears, and people pass them along because they resonate and because they feel like warnings to loved ones. Regionalizing a legend to a local place, such as a Seattle neighborhood or East Lake, makes it more vivid and more believable.

segments.title: Hallmarks of urban legends and the elevator story
segments.summary: The hosts list signs of an urban legend, starting with the friend-of-a-friend claim, and say legends often mention news topics. They recount the Eddie Murphy, Reggie Jackson, or Lionel Richie elevator-and-dog story and how its details vary by teller.

segments.title: News, movies and the history of folklore
segments.summary: Legends often spin off real news stories, such as a census-worker murder rumor, and the news can lend them credibility. Movies and TV also use or spread legends, such as Good Will Hunting and The Simpsons. The hosts discuss the difficulty of tracing origins and the folklore research of Jan Harold Brunvand, with earlier references to contemporary legends in the 1920s and 1890s.

segments.title: Snopes, real origins and Halloween candy
segments.summary: Real facts can seed legends, such as LSD-laced temporary tattoos. The hosts discuss Snopes, which gets angry emails from people defending their friends' stories. They discuss Halloween poisoned-candy legends, noting that most razor-blade cases were hoaxes, while one real case involved a child's heroin overdose.

segments.title: Forwarded email hoaxes
segments.summary: The hosts describe dead giveaways in forwarded emails and the Neiman Marcus cookie recipe hoax, which they say was falsely attributed to that store. They also discuss the birther email that Josh's dad forwarded, and say email-based legends lack the personalization of oral tradition.

segments.title: Real strange stories: hotel corpse and Elmer McCurdy
segments.summary: The hosts share urban legends that turn out to be true, including a couple who spent a night with a body under the bed, a hanging decoration that was a real body, and the Elmer McCurdy mummy that was displayed at carnivals and ended up in a Long Beach fun house. They cite Cracked and Snopes as sources.

segments.title: Plugs and sign-off
segments.summary: Instead of listener mail, the hosts plug sister podcasts and blogs, including Stuff from the Science Lab, Tech Stuff, Stuff You Missed in History Class, and Stuff Mom Never Told You, and invite emails to the show address.
